source: Bastardi & Shafir (1998) On the pursuit and misuse of useless information, Exp: course registration
finding: Waiting for information that would not change the choice changes the choice. In the course scenario, people who waited then mostly declined.
numbers: Simple version n=140: 82% register. Uncertain version n=149: 56% waited, 42% registered at once, 2% declined at once; many waiters declined, so only 71% in total registered vs 82%.
limits: Hypothetical choice; one scenario.
agent_relevance: An agent that asks for a test it does not need may then over-weight the result. Gate every test by whether any outcome could flip the action.

source: Bastardi & Shafir (1998) college admissions and mortgage problems
finding: Same pattern in admissions and mortgage choices; useless information shifts decisions toward the bad-news side.
numbers: Admissions: simple n=261, 43% reject; uncertain n=278, 74% waited and total reject was 54% (chi2(1,N=539)=6.15). Mortgage: simple approve 29%; uncertain 75% waited, total approve 56% (chi2=17.65, N=233). Waiters approved 72% when debt was $5,000, but only 29% in the simple version.
limits: Hypothetical; students.
agent_relevance: Check, before buying a test, what the best action would be for each possible result. If the same, the test is worthless (EVSI = 0).

source: Bastardi & Shafir (1998) CD player scenario and resolved-uncertainty control
finding: A control shows the pursuit itself, not just the mention of uncertainty, causes the shift.
numbers: Simple (known $90 repair): 91% buy. Uncertain with option to wait: 55% buy in total, 69% waited. Uncertainty resolved without pursuit (n=161): 75% buy. 91% vs 74% buy, chi2(1,N=336)=12.57.
limits: Wait rates were similar in the uncertain and resolved versions (69% vs 70%).
agent_relevance: Rules out the rival account that mentioning uncertainty hints at relevance. The effect is self-perception after acting.

source: Bastardi & Shafir (1998) wait rates when information cannot matter
finding: People wait for information even when logic says it cannot matter.
numbers: If repair cost is uncertain between $0 and $90, 70% wait. If between $90 and $180 (both above the buy threshold, so waiting is useless), 92% wait. Other variants: 66% and 60% wait ($50 vs $90, $50 vs $25).
limits: Hypothetical.
agent_relevance: Humans overbuy information. A scaffold copying human habits would inherit this; EVSI-style gating counters it.

source: Bastardi & Shafir (1998) tape-player raffle (real decision)
finding: The effect holds with real stakes. A real raffle with fee $10 or $30 (announced later) cut entry.
numbers: Simple condition knew $30: 57% enter. Uncertain condition: only 14% entered at once, 23% in total (chi2(1,N=45)=5.35, p<.03); over 70% of waiters declined once told $30.
limits: Small N=45; students.
agent_relevance: Real-payoff replication of the hypothetical results.

source: Bastardi & Shafir (1998) predictions about other decision makers
finding: People do not foresee the effect in others, which suggests it is not deliberate.
numbers: 70% predicted that a loan officer who waited would approve at $5,000 (observed 72%); only 20% predicted approval in the simple version (observed 29%). Admissions: 82% predicted rejection after a B in one group, 40% in another.
limits: Prediction tasks were separate groups.
agent_relevance: Models and people may not notice when tests are non-diagnostic. Needs an explicit check.

source: Brunswik Society newsletter (2003) cross-cultural replication of useless-information pursuit
finding: Reported a replication of the Bastardi-Shafir paradigm in three cultures.
numbers: 144 American, Iranian and Japanese participants over two surveys; all three groups pursued useless information (from a search snippet only; percentages not read).
limits: Not opened; snippet only. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Suggests the bias is not tied to one culture.

source: Dong et al. (2026) Value of Information: A Framework for Human-Agent Communication, main results
finding: An agent that computes the expected utility gain of a question minus its cost beats or matches tuned thresholds, with no tuning.
numbers: Models GPT-4.1 and Gemini-2.5-Flash; tasks Mixed 20Q, Flight Recommendation, Ambiguous WebShop. Mixed 20Q, cost 0.01: VoI utility 14.14 vs best tuned confidence-threshold baseline 11.49 (threshold 0.90).
limits: Belief over latent states is the LLM's own estimate; linear cost model; no ground-truth distribution.
agent_relevance: Direct template for an EVSI gate: ask only when expected gain exceeds cost. Main strength is no threshold tuning.

source: Dong et al. (2026) cost sweep ablation (Gemini-2.5-Flash, Mixed 20Q)
finding: The VoI controller wins at most costs but not all; at cost 0.10 it loses to the best tuned baseline.
numbers: Reward VoI vs best baseline (grid of 9 settings): cost 0.01 8.64 vs 8.30; 0.02 7.72 vs 6.88; 0.05 5.01 vs 3.65 (+1.36, the headline gain); 0.10 1.38 vs 2.28 (-0.90); 0.20 -0.96 vs 0 (No Question wins).
limits: Baselines were tuned per cost; VoI untuned. Single model for this table.
agent_relevance: Failure case: when cost is high, the correct move is to ask nothing, yet VoI still asks a little. Add a stop floor.

source: Dong et al. (2026) rival strategies: fixed rounds, adaptive prompting, confidence threshold
finding: Fixed-round asking gives an inverted U in utility. Telling the model to ask when needed is inconsistent. Confidence thresholds work only if tuned per task and cost.
numbers: Utility rises then falls with the number of questions as cost accumulates; confidence-threshold can match VoI on GPT-4 Mixed 20Q and WebShop but the best threshold varies (0.5 to 0.9 across costs).
limits: Qualitative text claims; numbers in figures.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code question counts; compute the stop rule from gain versus cost.

source: Dong et al. (2026) calibration of the LLM belief used for VoI
finding: VoI is only as good as the model's probabilities. Calibration was fair for animal guessing, poorer for medical diagnosis.
numbers: Measured as argmax accuracy vs predicted probability (Figure 3) for GPT-4 and Gemini-2.5-Flash on animal guessing, medical diagnosis and flight recommendation; no ground-truth distribution available.
limits: Authors could not compare to a true distribution.
agent_relevance: Test quality (noisy test) enters EVSI via the likelihood; a miscalibrated likelihood misprices the test. Coherence checks (G5) matter.

source: Ding et al. (2026) Calibrate-Then-Act: Cost-Aware Exploration in LLM Agents, Pandora's Box
finding: Giving the LLM explicit priors and costs lets it nearly match the optimal explore-or-commit policy.
numbers: Qwen3-8B, 100 Pandora's Box items: optimal-match 94% for CTA-Prompted vs 23% prompted without priors; reward 0.625 vs oracle 0.649 vs 0.476. Without thinking: 20% and 11%.
limits: Toy setting; one 8B model.
agent_relevance: Supports passing prior and cost to the model as data and letting code do the comparison.

source: Ding et al. (2026) CTA, retrieval (PopQA) task
finding: Retrieval is a costly noisy test. Always retrieving loses to never retrieving once cost counts; calibrated choice is best.
numbers: 1,000 PopQA questions, Qwen3-8B: Never retrieve acc 0.226 reward 0.226; Always retrieve acc 0.578 reward 0.213; Prompted 61% retrieve reward 0.283; CTA-Prompted 65.3% retrieve reward 0.293. Isotonic calibration cut ECE from 0.618 to 0.029.
limits: Single dataset; modest gain 0.283 to 0.293.
agent_relevance: Always-test can be worse than never-test after cost; calibration of confidence is the enabling step.

source: Ding et al. (2026) CTA, code task (FileReading) with RL
finding: Adding priors to RL adds a small gain; RL alone never learned to skip tests.
numbers: 2,000 tasks, four cost ratios: reward Prompted 0.229, CTA-Prompted 0.240, RL 0.259, CTA-RL 0.268 (about 3.5% over RL). Unit tests per task 2.13 (RL) vs 1.98 (CTA-RL). RL never chose guess-and-go (0%).
limits: Format predictor BERT-tiny only 67% accurate; simplified task.
agent_relevance: Small effect when the environment is easy; benefit comes from cost awareness.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: Choosing the question with the highest expected information gain, by simulating answers, raises success.
numbers: Average success-rate gain 38.1% over direct prompting across 5 datasets and 5 LLMs; Llama3-70B +46.6%; GPT-4 DX 89.4 to 97.0, MedDG 74.9 to 87.9, FloDial 42.5 to 67.8, Common 49.0 to 70.9, Thing 30.8 to 36.8.
limits: Closed-set elimination setting; answers assumed to rule out sets fully; authors note a simplified benchmark.
agent_relevance: Entropy-based question value is cheap and works. The test is treated as noise-free, so it is EVPI-like, not full EVSI.

source: Hu et al. (2024) UoT comparison with other planners and ablations
finding: The information-gain reward beats generic search prompts; the gain over plain tree search is smaller than over direct prompting.
numbers: UoT beats CoT-SC by 33.8 points, Reflexion by 29.9, original ToT by 28.3, adapted ToT by 12.4; pruned UoT beats adapted ToT by 7.36. GPT-4 troubleshooting 43.7 to 67.3. Paired t-tests all p<0.05 (Tables 7 and 8, few runs).
limits: Few runs; compute grows with simulation depth (limited to 3 steps).
agent_relevance: Most of the benefit comes from the principled reward, not search depth.

source: Li, Jalal & Heath (2024) Accurate EVSI Estimation for Nonlinear Models Using the Gaussian Approximation Method
finding: Fast EVSI approximations can be badly wrong for nonlinear models; a Taylor-series-plus-Gaussian method fixes this.
numbers: Case I: conventional Gaussian approximation largely overestimates EVSI; spline-Taylor method overlaps the analytic result. Time 354.85 s (GA), 16.86 s (new), 101.04 s (nonparametric). Case II: nested Monte Carlo about 6 h on 16 cores per estimate; new method 1.86 s; nonparametric 1,216 s; new method less accurate than regression for n<30.
limits: Needs Fisher information; small-sample accuracy lower.
agent_relevance: Cheap value-of-test formulas can mislead when payoff is nonlinear; check against exact enumeration in small agent problems.

source: Li et al. (2025) Nonparametric estimation of effective sample size in Gaussian approximation of EVSI
finding: The prior strength n0 needed by Gaussian EVSI can be estimated by regression instead of slow MCMC.
numbers: Experiments 1 to 4 analytic n0 10, 20, 100, 23: regression gave 10.00, 20.92, 98.83, 23.12; summary-statistics method overestimated Exp 2 (24.17 vs 20). MCMC took 3.3 to 285 min, regression about 0.01 min in six of seven cases.
limits: Needs a large training sample; relies on a good summary statistic.
agent_relevance: Prior weight (how many samples the prior is worth) controls how much a test can shift belief.

source: Breeze et al. (2025) Value for money of 24 randomised trial designs for weight management programmes
finding: EVSI net of trial cost ranks designs; half of the 24 designs had negative net value.
numbers: Per-person EVSI 6.84 to 29.39 GBP; trial costs 1.54m to 2.57m GBP; 12 of 24 designs had positive ENBS; best design (2-year, n=2,000, all programmes) ENBS 13.24m GBP.
limits: Only 4 experts elicited; regression EVSI with 3,000 PSA runs; no comparison with a power-based calculation.
agent_relevance: Net value can be negative: a test can cost more than its information. Needs a built-in no-test option.

source: Pei et al. (2023) Value of information and value of implementation, HIV-associated TB diagnostic trials
finding: Information has no value when the decision is not close; implementation value can dwarf information value.
numbers: Trial of 2,600 per arm: EVSI $900,000 at $780/YLS but $0 at $3,000/YLS; value of implementation at $3,000/YLS about $654 million. Urine test sensitivity FujiLAM 62%/23% vs AlereLAM 48%/2% by CD4 group.
limits: Trial costs not included; value sensitive near the $780/YLS threshold; uptake assumptions untested.
agent_relevance: EVSI is zero if the current best action is robust to the sample; value is highest near a decision boundary.

source: Chen et al. (2026) How accurate should a precision medical test be to meet cost-effectiveness
finding: Derives the minimum accuracy of a noisy test for it to be worth using; rare classes need accuracy near 1.
numbers: Theorems give local and global accuracy bounds that rise with test cost; with equal accuracies the bound is above 50%; 4-class example prevalences 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40; 200 random scenarios in simulation.
limits: Deterministic outcomes within each class; hard classification; no sequential testing; theory, not policy.
agent_relevance: Gives a ready rule: a test must beat a prevalence-weighted bound or be skipped.

source: Vervaart (2024) Calculating the Expected Net Benefit of Sampling for survival data: tutorial
finding: ENBS for follow-up length shows when more data pay off; the case study picks 18 months extra follow-up.
numbers: KEYNOTE-426: 861 enrolled, 156 (18%) deaths of target 404 (47%); WTP 30,000 GBP/QALY; 5,000 simulations; fixed reappraisal cost 100,000 GBP; optimal 18 months extra follow-up; scenario changes flipped the best option.
limits: Reconstructed KM data; independence assumption; conclusion sensitive to reversal probability.
agent_relevance: Optimum depends on assumptions about what will be done with the data; sensitivity analysis needed.

source: Raiffa & Schlaifer (1961) Applied Statistical Decision Theory
finding: Founding text defining the expected value of sample information and preposterior analysis.
numbers: Not opened this session; no numbers recorded.
limits: Memory-based; verify before use.
agent_relevance: EVSI = expected value of deciding after seeing the sample minus value of deciding now; bounded above by EVPI.

source: Strong, Oakley & Brennan (2014) Estimating multiparameter partial EVPI from a probabilistic sensitivity analysis sample: a nonparametric regression approach
finding: Regression on a single probabilistic sensitivity run replaced nested Monte Carlo for partial EVPI; the EVSI extension followed.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: Memory-based; verify before use.
agent_relevance: Regression shortcuts are why the 2024-25 methods above exist.

source: Bastardi & Shafir (1998) explanation: pursuit makes the information seem instrumental
finding: Authors argue people rarely know they are pursuing useless information. Having sought it, they treat it as decisive (self-perception, contrast, reactance are rival or added accounts).
numbers: Supporting data: wait rates were 69% vs 70% whether waiting was tied to the information or incidental, yet only the former shifted choice (CD player: 75% buy resolved vs 55% buy uncertain).
limits: Mechanism is argued, not directly measured; the paper itself lists several mutually compatible accounts.
agent_relevance: Order matters: compute whether any result could change the action before running the test, not after seeing it.
